section.title: Doing Good and Avoiding Divisions
section.sectionRationale: Paul turns to the believer's life in society: submission to authorities, gentleness toward all, and readiness for every good work. He grounds this in a stunning gospel remembrance, we too were once enslaved to sin, but God our Savior saved us by His mercy through the washing of regeneration, and closes by urging devotion to good and the rejection of divisive, pointless quarrels.
section.thesis: Because God saved us by His kindness and mercy, not by our righteous deeds, washing and renewing us by the Spirit and justifying us by grace, we are freed to live gently and do good in the world, avoiding the empty controversies and divisions that destroy.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the call to good citizenship and gentleness; the gospel ground, remembering what we were and the mercy that saved us through the washing of regeneration; and the charge to devote ourselves to good works while rejecting divisive people and worthless quarrels.

verses.text: Remind the believers to submit to rulers and authorities, to be obedient and ready for every good work,
to malign no one, and to be peaceable and gentle, showing full consideration to everyone.
For at one time we too were foolish, disobedient, misled, and enslaved to all sorts of desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, being hated and hating one another.

units.label: But God our Savior saved us

verses.text: But when the {{chrestotes|kindness}} of God our Savior and His {{philanthropia|love for mankind}} appeared,
He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy, through the washing of {{palingenesia|new birth}} and {{anakainosis|renewal}} by the Holy Spirit.
This is the Spirit He poured out on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior,
so that, having been {{dikaioo|justified}} by His grace, we would become heirs with the hope of eternal life.

units.label: Devote yourself to good, avoid divisions

verses.text: This saying is trustworthy. And I want you to emphasize these things, so that those who have believed God will take care to devote themselves to good deeds. These things are excellent and profitable for the people.
But avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, arguments, and quarrels about the law, because these things are pointless and worthless.
Reject a {{hairetikos|divisive}} man after a first and second admonition,
knowing that such a man is corrupt and sinful; he is self-condemned.

chrestotes.gloss: Kindness, goodness, generous benevolence in action. It names the warm, gracious disposition of God our Saviour that appeared in Christ. Paired with His love for mankind, it stresses that salvation flows not from our merit but from the sheer kindness of God's heart toward undeserving people.

philanthropia.gloss: Love for mankind, benevolence toward humanity, the root of our word philanthropy. Applied to God, it describes His affectionate goodwill toward people. That this appeared, like the grace of chapter 2, points to the coming of Christ, in whom God's love for humanity took visible, saving form.

palingenesia.gloss: New birth, regeneration, a being born again. Used only twice in the New Testament, here of the believer's rebirth and in Matthew 19:28 of the renewal of all things. The washing of regeneration pictures the cleansing, life-giving work of the Spirit that makes a sinner new, as the BSB footnote notes, rendering it of regeneration.

anakainosis.gloss: Renewal, a making new again. It describes the Spirit's ongoing work of transforming the believer, closely joined here to the new birth. Together, washing, regeneration, and renewal portray salvation as a thorough inward renovation worked by the Holy Spirit, not a mere improvement of the old self.

dikaioo.gloss: To justify, to declare righteous. A key term of Paul's gospel: God counts the believer righteous by grace, on the basis of Christ, not their deeds. Here justification by His grace makes us heirs with the hope of eternal life, tying the legal verdict to the family inheritance.

hairetikos.gloss: Divisive, factious, given to causing splits, the root of our word heretic. It describes a person who stirs up parties and division in the church, often around the pointless controversies just mentioned. After patient warning, such a person is to be rejected, for their persistence exposes a corrupt and self-condemned heart.

basic.context: Paul tells Titus to remind believers how to live in the wider world: respecting authorities, doing good, speaking well of others, and being gentle to everyone. Then he explains why we can live this way: we were once trapped in sin ourselves, but God saved us out of pure kindness and mercy, washing and renewing us by His Spirit. He ends by urging devotion to good works and warning against people who cause needless division.
basic.hermeneutics: Verses 4-7 are one of the great gospel summaries in the Bible, spelling out that salvation is God's work by mercy, not ours by merit. The washing of regeneration describes the Spirit's cleansing, life-giving work; Christians differ on how it relates to baptism, but the emphasis is on God's saving act. The warnings about quarrels and divisive people are practical guardrails around a healthy church.
basic.originalLanguages: God's chrestotes, kindness, and His philanthropia, love for mankind, appeared in Christ. He saved us through the washing of palingenesia, new birth or regeneration, and anakainosis, renewal, by the Spirit. Having been dikaioo, justified, by grace, we became heirs. A divisive person, hairetikos, is to be rejected after warnings.
basic.typology: The washing of regeneration recalls the many Old Testament cleansings and the promise in Ezekiel that God would sprinkle clean water on His people and give them a new heart and His Spirit. Christ fulfils these shadows, cleansing and renewing His people inwardly.
basic.christ: God's kindness and love appeared in Jesus, our Saviour, echoing the appearing of grace in chapter 2. Through Him the Spirit is poured out abundantly, and by His grace we are justified and made heirs of eternal life. Salvation from first to last is centred on Christ and applied by the Spirit.
basic.god: God is our Saviour, kind and loving toward humanity, rich in mercy. He saves not because of our righteous deeds but because of His mercy, pouring out His Spirit generously and justifying us by grace. He is a generous God who makes enemies into heirs.
basic.crossReferences: Ephesians 2 describes the same movement from dead in sin to saved by grace. Ezekiel 36 promises cleansing with water and a new heart by God's Spirit. And Romans 5 shows justification by grace leading to hope, just as here.
basic.oneStory: Here is the gospel in miniature: humanity enslaved to sin, then rescued purely by God's kindness and mercy, washed and renewed by the Spirit, justified by grace, and made heirs of eternal life. It is the same salvation promised through the prophets and secured in Christ, now producing a people who devote themselves to doing good in the world.

context.literary:
The paragraph is built like a hinge. Verses 1 and 2 give a rapid list of eight attitudes toward the world, ending with the sweeping phrase to everyone. Verse 3 then supplies the reason in the form of a memory: for at one time we too were. It lists the old life in six phrases, foolish, disobedient, misled, enslaved, living in malice and envy, hated and hating, and verse 4 breaks it with two small words, but when. The sentence that follows, running from verse 4 through verse 7, is a single long statement in Greek, with the saving work of the Father, the Spirit and the Son all contained in it.

The structure of that sentence is easy to hear. It opens with God's kindness appearing, states the negative, not by deeds of righteousness, then the positive, according to His mercy, then the means, washing and renewal by the Spirit, then the abundance of the pouring out through Jesus Christ, and finally two results, that we would be justified and become heirs. The big purpose clause of verse 7 ends with hope of eternal life, which brings the reader back to the opening of the letter, 1:2.

Verse 8 follows with the formula this saying is trustworthy, and the section turns again to practice: be careful to devote yourselves to good works. The final three verses then turn to the opposite problem, the foolish controversies and the divisive man. The chapter's rhythm is practice, gospel, practice, and the warnings fill the space left by a church that has understood what it was saved for.
context.historical:
Crete was a Roman province, and the believers there lived under governors, taxes and local magistrates. Christians met in homes and were a small minority in a society proud of its gods and its city traditions. Paul tells them to be submissive and obedient to rulers, and to be ready for every good work. He gives the same counsel in Romans 13:1-7 and 1 Timothy 2:1-2, and Peter does the same in 1 Peter 2:13-17. In an age when new movements were easily suspected, quiet submission and good deeds closed the mouths of critics.

The list of the old life in verse 3 describes a world Paul's readers knew first hand. Greek and Roman moralists wrote about the passions that ruled people and about the hatred and envy in cities, and Paul's description would have rung true. The believers on Crete were from the same stock that gave the island a bad name, and the verse insists that Paul and Titus were no better: we too were. It is a deliberate refusal to stand above the people being taught.

The controversies of verse 9 reflect the agenda of the teachers described in chapter 1: Jewish myths, endless genealogies and quarrels about the law. Such speculation was popular in some Jewish circles and drew on the stories of the Old Testament, with long lines of descent as a source for secret teaching. Paul calls it pointless and worthless. Dealing with a divisive man by two warnings and then separation matches a pattern Jesus set in Matthew 18:15-17 and that Paul applied in Romans 16:17 and 2 Thessalonians 3:14-15.
context.canonical:
Titus 3:4-7 is one of the central salvation texts in the New Testament, ranking beside Ephesians 2:4-10, Romans 3:21-26 and 2 Timothy 1:9-10. It resembles the last of these closely, with the same elements: God our Savior, salvation not on the basis of works, grace, and the appearing of Christ. It is also one of the clearest passages where the three persons of the Godhead act together to save, with the Father sending, the Spirit renewing, and the Son as the channel.

The background of the passage runs through the Old Testament. Ezekiel 36:25-27 promised that God would sprinkle clean water on His people, cleanse them from their idols and give them a new heart and a new spirit within them. Joel 2:28-29 promised that He would pour out His Spirit on all flesh. Deuteronomy 9:4-6 warned Israel that the land was not given because of their righteousness, a text that matches the not by deeds of righteousness of verse 5. Jesus told Nicodemus that no one can enter the kingdom without being born of water and the Spirit, John 3:5-8, expecting him to know Ezekiel.

The New Testament takes up the language in several places. Paul reminds the Corinthians that some of them had been wicked, but they were washed, sanctified and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit of our God, 1 Corinthians 6:9-11. Peter speaks of being born again to a living hope, 1 Peter 1:3, and Paul speaks of the washing of water with the word in Ephesians 5:26. The word regeneration also appears in Matthew 19:28, for the renewal of all things at the Son of Man's throne.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul is writing a manual for life in a hostile or indifferent world, and he wants Titus to understand how the gospel shapes the way believers deal with outsiders. The first two verses call for a posture of cooperation and courtesy: submit, be obedient, be ready, speak no evil, be peaceable, be gentle. This is not weakness. It is the pressure of grace, since people who know they were rescued from the same pit have no basis for contempt.

The memory of verse 3 does a particular job. It blocks any sense of superiority. Paul wants the Cretans, who were proverbial for vices, to see that the difference between them and their neighbours is not breeding or effort but mercy. The same thing would be said of Paul and Titus. Verses 4 to 7 give that mercy its full weight in order to make the call to good works an act of gratitude rather than an attempt to earn something.

The last part of the passage has a more specific aim. Paul does not want the church to waste its energy on speculation and arguments about the law, which produce nothing. He wants it to put its strength into useful works, and he wants Titus to deal with people who keep splitting the church, giving them every chance and then, if they refuse, letting them go. The first hearers would have understood that the gospel of grace and the discipline of the church belong together.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Verses 4 to 7 describe what God has done, and they are the doctrinal core of the passage: they are not commands. Nothing in them asks readers to earn salvation, and they cannot be turned into a method. The commands are in verses 1 and 2, the call to submit, be ready for good work and show gentleness, and verses 8 to 10, devote yourselves to good works, avoid foolish controversies and deal with the divisive. These are prescriptive for the church in every age.

Some care is needed. The command to submit to rulers is real, but Scripture elsewhere shows that obedience to God comes first when rulers demand what He forbids, as in Acts 5:29 and Daniel 3 and 6. The call to reject a divisive man applies to the person who keeps stirring factions after repeated correction. It is not a licence to expel anyone who disagrees. Paul says first and second warnings, and elsewhere he treats those under discipline as brothers to be warned, 2 Thessalonians 3:15. Finally, the passage says nothing of a Christian life being optional: those who have believed God are to take care to devote themselves to good deeds, verse 8, and that is a continuing obligation.

debates.question: What is the washing of regeneration in verse 5?

views.label: The Spirit's inward cleansing and new birth
views.case: On this reading the washing is a picture of what the Spirit does within, fulfilling the promise of Ezekiel 36:25-27 of clean water and a new heart. The phrase renewal by the Holy Spirit explains it, and salvation is described as God's act and not a ritual. John 3:5 and 1 Corinthians 6:11 are read the same way.

views.label: A washing that includes baptism
views.case: Others hold that the word washing, which Ephesians 5:26 also uses, points to baptism as the visible sign that goes with the Spirit's work. Some in the church's history have taken baptism to be the moment when regeneration is given, while others see it as the sign and seal of grace already given. Acts 22:16 and 1 Peter 3:21 are cited in support.

debates.bearing: Every view agrees that the source of salvation is God's mercy through the Spirit and not human deeds. The disagreement is about how closely the outward sign and the inward gift are tied. The context points to the inward work, since the verse is intended to exclude any contribution by works.

debates.question: Does 'this saying is trustworthy' look back or ahead?

views.label: It affirms the gospel summary just given
views.case: Paul uses the formula in the Pastorals for a short statement that readers can hold with confidence, as in 1 Timothy 1:15 and 2 Timothy 2:11. Placed after the long sentence of verses 4 to 7, it seals that statement as a creed-like saying.

views.label: It introduces the call to good works
views.case: The line may point forward to the instruction that follows, so that the trustworthy saying is the command to devote oneself to good deeds. In 1 Timothy 3:1 the formula introduces a statement that follows.

debates.bearing: The two readings hold together, since verse 8 joins the gospel to its fruit: because these things are true, believers must take care to do good. Either way, doctrine and duty are tied in one breath.

debates.question: Is the divisive man someone to expel, or someone to avoid?

views.label: Formal removal from the church
views.case: The word reject suggests refusing fellowship after two warnings, in line with Matthew 18:15-17 and 1 Corinthians 5:9-13, so the church acts together to protect itself from a persistent factionalist.

views.label: Withdrawal of association
views.case: Others say Paul means that Titus and the church should refuse to be drawn into the person's disputes and stop treating him as a partner in ministry, as in 2 Timothy 2:23-25, where patient correction of opponents continues in the hope of repentance.

debates.bearing: What matters is the sequence. Patient warning comes first, repeated, and only the person who will not hear is set aside. The self-condemned man has in effect chosen it, and the purpose remains the person's recovery.

study.originalLanguages:
The first two verses contain words that are easily lost. The word translated full consideration in the BSB, prautes, is more often rendered gentleness or meekness. It is one of the fruits of the Spirit, Galatians 5:23, and Paul asks that those who oppose be corrected with it, 2 Timothy 2:25. The verb for malign in verse 2 is blasphemeo, the root of blasphemy, so Paul is saying: do not blaspheme anyone, do not slander. The word translated peaceable, amachos, means not a fighter. These three, along with gentleness, are a character profile of the person who knows he has received mercy.

Verse 3 lists the old life with sharp words. Foolish, anoetos, means without understanding, and misled, planao, means wandering. Enslaved, douleuo, is the word for slavery, applied to desires and pleasures, a theme close to Romans 6:16-20. Hated and hating, stugetos and miseo, paint a social poison. It is a mirror of the Cretan reputation of chapter 1, now applied to all.

Verse 4 pairs two words for God's character, chrestotes and philanthropia, and both appear in this chapter as qualities that have shown themselves in Christ. The second is the origin of philanthropy, love for humankind, and Luke uses it of the kindness of the islanders of Malta, Acts 28:2. For Paul, the great philanthropist is God.

In verse 5, the word for washing, loutron, is the one Paul uses in Ephesians 5:26, and it refers to a bath or the place of washing. Regeneration, palingenesia, means a new beginning or birth again, and outside this verse the only place it is used in the New Testament is Matthew 19:28, for the renewal of the world when the Son of Man sits on His throne. Paul applies a cosmic word to a personal event. Renewal, anakainosis, is the word of Romans 12:2, the renewing of the mind. Paul says the Spirit does both.

The verb poured out in verse 6, ekcheo, is the verb of Joel's promise that God would pour out His Spirit, as Acts 2:17 and 2:33 quote it, and it is joined with the adverb richly, so the gift is lavish. Verse 7 uses the aorist passive participle dikaiotheis, having been justified, so the action is completed and done to us, not by us. Heirs according to the hope of eternal life ties the verse to 1:2.

Finally, devote yourselves in verses 8 and 14 is the verb proistemi, to stand before, lead or care for. In 1 Timothy 3:4 and 5:17 it describes elders who manage, so every believer is to give oversight to good works the way an elder oversees a household. And the divisive man of verse 10 comes from hairesis, a party, and reject is paraiteomai, to refuse, the word used of foolish myths in 1 Timothy 4:7.

typology.type: Clean water and a new heart, verse 5
typology.fulfillment: Ezekiel promised that God would sprinkle clean water on His people to cleanse them from all their uncleanness and idols, and would give them a new heart and put His Spirit within them, Ezekiel 36:25-27. Priests were washed at their consecration, Exodus 29:4, and the bronze basin stood for cleansing before service, Exodus 30:17-21. Titus sees the promise realised: the Spirit is poured out through Jesus Christ and the washing is of new birth. The escalation is from outward cleansing that had to be repeated to an inward renewal that begins a new life. The type is not yet complete, since the renewal of the body and the world is still to come, Romans 8:23.

A foreign commander, proud and diseased, is told to wash in the Jordan, and when he does his flesh is restored like that of a young boy, 2 Kings 5:10-14. He did nothing to deserve it and nearly refused the simple remedy. The story is a picture of the way Titus describes salvation: a washing that makes a person new, received by the humble and not by the strong, apart from their own deeds. Jesus Himself points to Naaman in Luke 4:27. The correspondence is that of a healing by grace, but Naaman was healed of a body and Christ gives new birth to the whole person.

typology.type: Not because of righteousness: Israel and the land
typology.fulfillment: God warned Israel that He was giving them the land not because of their righteousness, for they were a stiff necked people, but because of His promise and the wickedness of the nations, Deuteronomy 9:4-6. The inheritance was a gift. Titus says the same of the greater inheritance: God saved us not by deeds of righteousness, but according to His mercy, and made us heirs, verse 7. Paul draws the link between the promise and the heirs in Romans 4:13 and Galatians 3:29. The land was a shadow, and the inheritance in Christ is eternal life and the renewed creation. The type falls short because the land could be lost, while the inheritance of grace is kept by God.

typology.type: The pouring out of the Spirit
typology.fulfillment: Joel promised that in the last days God would pour out His Spirit on all flesh, Joel 2:28-29, and the earlier prophets pictured water poured on thirsty ground, Isaiah 44:3. Peter explained Pentecost as the fulfilment, with the Spirit poured out by the risen and exalted Jesus, Acts 2:32-33. Titus says the Spirit was poured out abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so the gift reaches ordinary believers in Crete. The pattern grows from a gift to a few prophets, judges and kings to a gift to every believer. It is still unfolding in the church, awaiting the full redemption of our bodies.

study.christ:
Titus 3 gives one of the most concentrated pictures of Christ's place in salvation. The first thing it says is that the kindness and love of God our Savior appeared. Verse 4 uses the same verb as 2:11, and the appearing is Jesus. The one whom the world met in Galilee was the visible form of God's kindness toward people who were hostile and hating, verse 3. When Jesus ate with sinners and touched lepers He was acting out what verse 4 says in words.

Second, the Spirit comes through Him. The Spirit is poured out through Jesus Christ our Savior, verse 6, so the new birth and renewal that Paul describes are not an independent work but a gift from the risen Lord. Acts 2:33 says the exalted Jesus received the promised Spirit from the Father and poured Him out. It is notable that Paul calls both the Father in verse 4 and Jesus in verse 6 Savior, a pairing that makes sense only if the Son shares in the saving work of God.

Third, justification is by His grace. Verse 7 says that we have been justified by His grace, and the pronoun fits Christ as well as the Father. Justification means being declared right with God, and Paul has taught elsewhere that it rests on Christ's righteousness and His death, Romans 3:24-26 and 5:9. The text here does not say how, since it assumes the answer in 2:14: He gave Himself for us. The mercy of verse 5 passes through His cross.

Fourth, heirs. To be an heir with hope of eternal life is to share in what belongs to Christ, who is the heir of all things, Hebrews 1:2. Paul says that we are fellow heirs with Him, Romans 8:17, and so the believer enters a family inheritance because of a relationship with the Son.

Finally, Christ is the one who removes the grounds for boasting and so for division. The foolish controversies of verse 9 and the divisive man of verse 10 are set against the man who knows he was saved by mercy. A church that understands that Christ gave Himself for people who were foolish and hating will find it hard to hold a grudge. It also helps to keep from forced links: the passage does not ask us to find Christ in every detail of the washing, but it places Him at the centre of the sentence in which the whole Trinity acts.
study.god:
The passage shows the Triune God at work in a single sentence. God our Savior is the author and source: His kindness appeared and He saved us, verses 4 and 5. The Holy Spirit is the one who washes and renews, verse 5, and who is poured out richly, verse 6. Jesus Christ our Savior is the one through whom the Spirit comes, verse 6. Without any abstract argument, Paul reveals a God in whom Father, Son and Spirit have each a distinct role in the rescue of a people. Salvation is a work of the whole Godhead.

The character that shines is kindness. The two words of verse 4 present a God who is good and who loves humankind. It is notable that this goodness is displayed not toward people who were beautiful but toward people who were foolish, disobedient and hating, verse 3. He is not like the gods of the Cretan myths, who were petty and moody. He loves those who do not deserve it, and His mercy is the reason for what He does, not our deeds.

He is a God of generosity. The Spirit is poured out abundantly, the verb for pouring and the word richly both stress excess. He does not give the Spirit grudgingly or in measured portions. The inheritance of eternal life is also given freely, and a God who makes heirs out of rebels is lavish.

He is a God who justifies. The verdict of verse 7 does not describe a legal fiction or a reward for good behaviour: He declares righteous those who are guilty, and He does so by grace. The holiness of God is not lowered, but it is met in Christ.

He is a God who cares about the good of the world. Believers are to be ready for every good work and to do good to everyone because their God does good to the undeserving. The mercy shown to them is the model for the way they live among their neighbours.

For worship, the passage calls us to humility and praise. It denies us any ground for pride and gives us every ground for thanks. It also invites us to treat the people around us as God treated us. A congregation that knows what it was saved from will be quick to show kindness and slow to fight over trifles.

crossReferences.note: Paul describes people dead in trespasses, following the course of this world, then made alive with Christ by grace through faith, not by works, and created for good works. It is the same movement as Titus 3:3-8: the old life, the intervention of mercy, and good works as the outcome and not the cause.

God promises to sprinkle clean water on His people, give them a new heart and put His Spirit within them. These promises stand behind the washing and renewal by the Holy Spirit in Titus 3:5, and show that Paul is announcing the fulfilment of an Old Testament hope in Christ.

Jesus tells Nicodemus that unless someone is born again, or from above, of water and the Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God. The idea of a new birth by the Spirit that Titus 3:5 calls palingenesia is the same truth in different words, and both texts say that the work is God's and not ours.

After listing the kinds of people who will not inherit the kingdom, Paul says that some of the Corinthians were such, but they were washed, sanctified and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit of our God. It mirrors Titus 3:3-7 in both the confession of a past life and the three terms of washing, Spirit and justification.

Paul explains that God's righteousness comes through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe and that people are justified freely by His grace through the redemption in Christ. It is the doctrinal expansion of Titus 3:7, and it shows how the verdict of justification rests on Christ's sacrifice.

Moses warns Israel not to think the Lord brings them into the land because of their righteousness, because they are a stubborn people. It is the Old Testament form of Titus 3:5, where salvation is not by deeds of righteousness we have done, and it shows that grace has always been the way God deals with His people.

Peter explains Pentecost as the fulfilment of Joel's promise that God would pour out His Spirit on all people. Titus 3:6 describes the same outpouring as abundant and through Jesus Christ, so the gift once reserved for a few is now given to every believer.

Jesus gives steps for dealing with a brother who sins: speak to him alone, then with witnesses, then the church. It is the pattern behind Titus 3:10, where a divisive man is given a first and second warning before the church distances itself, and it shows that patience and firmness belong together.

Paul tells Timothy to avoid foolish and ignorant controversies, which breed quarrels, and to correct opponents with gentleness in the hope that God may grant them repentance. It is the companion to Titus 3:9-11, and it explains that even the firm treatment of the divisive is aimed at their recovery.

Paul tells believers to be subject to the governing authorities, since there is no authority except from God. The basic call to submit and do good in Titus 3:1 comes from the same thinking, with a concern for the church's reputation and a trust that God rules over earthly powers.

study.oneStory:
Titus 3:3-7 sums up the story of the Bible in five verses. It begins with a humanity that is foolish, enslaved and hating, which is the condition that began in Genesis 3, when trust in God's word was exchanged for the serpent's lie. Everything in the following chapters of Genesis, with murder, violence and the scattering at Babel, shows the same slavery to desire and hatred.

The turn comes with but when. The Old Testament moves toward it with God's repeated mercy: Abraham called while his family served other gods, Joshua 24:2, Israel rescued from slavery in Egypt, and Israel brought into the land not for its righteousness, Deuteronomy 9:4-6. Each rescue was a preview. The prophets looked for a deeper one, in which God would wash His people, give them a new heart and put His Spirit within them, Ezekiel 36:25-27, and pour out His Spirit on all flesh, Joel 2:28.

Titus declares that this has happened. The kindness and love of God our Savior have appeared in Jesus, and the Spirit has been poured out through Him. The new creation has begun in the people who have been renewed. They are already heirs, but the inheritance is held in hope, and they live between the first appearing of grace and the final appearing of glory.

For now, these people are sent into the world to do good, to be gentle with everyone, and to avoid the quarrels that waste their energy. They do not stand above their neighbours. They remember what they were. The story ends in the renewal of all things, which the very word palingenesia names in Matthew 19:28, when the Son of Man sits on His glorious throne and the whole creation shares in the new birth. Revelation 21:5 gives the voice that says, behold, I am making all things new. What began as a washing for a few on Crete reaches as far as the new heaven and the new earth, and the heirs enter the inheritance of eternal life that God promised before the ages began, 1:2.

sermon.title: Jesus Christ Our Savior
sermon.why: From Begg's series A Study in Titus, this message expounds Titus 3:4-6, the appearing of God's kindness and love and salvation through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Spirit, the gospel heart of this movement. A clear, orthodox handling of the passage.

quiz.q: How does Paul say believers should live toward the wider world?

options.text: Submissive to authorities, ready for every good work, gentle and considerate to everyone.
options.note: Verses 1-2 call for good citizenship, good works, and gentleness.

options.text: Withdrawn and hostile toward outsiders.
options.note: The opposite; Paul urges peace, gentleness, and doing good to all.

options.text: Free to malign and quarrel with opponents.
options.note: Paul says to malign no one and to be peaceable.

options.text: Indifferent to how they are seen by others.
options.note: Their conduct is to commend the gospel before all.

quiz.q: What does Paul say we were like before God saved us?

options.text: Foolish, disobedient, misled, and enslaved to desires, living in malice and envy.
options.note: Verse 3 gives this sober portrait of our former state.

options.text: Basically good people who needed slight improvement.
options.note: Paul paints a picture of real bondage to sin, not minor faults.

options.text: Already righteous through our own efforts.
options.note: The point is that we were enslaved, not righteous.

options.text: Innocent victims with no sin of our own.
options.note: Paul names our own disobedience and malice, not mere victimhood.

quiz.q: On what basis did God save us, according to verse 5?

options.text: According to His mercy, not by the righteous deeds we had done.
options.note: Verse 5 explicitly excludes our works and rests salvation on His mercy.

options.text: Because we had earned it by good behaviour.
options.note: Paul directly denies this; it is not by our righteous deeds.

options.text: Because we were more deserving than others.
options.note: Salvation is by mercy, ruling out any deserving on our part.

options.text: Because we first cleaned ourselves up.
options.note: It is God who washes and renews us, not we ourselves.

quiz.q: What is the result of being justified by His grace?

options.text: We become heirs with the hope of eternal life.
options.note: Verse 7 links justification to the inheritance and hope.

options.text: We earn a temporary probation.
options.note: The gift is a secure inheritance and hope, not probation.

options.text: We are left uncertain of our standing.
options.note: Justification gives a settled hope, not uncertainty.

options.text: We must now save ourselves by works.
options.note: Justification is by grace; good works flow from it, not for it.

quiz.q: How does Paul say the church should handle a divisive person?

options.text: Warn him once and twice, then reject him if he persists.
options.note: Verses 10-11 allow patient warning, then rejection of the unrepentant.

options.text: Ignore the division entirely.
options.note: Patience is shown, but persistent division must finally be confronted.

options.text: Reject him instantly with no warning.
options.note: Paul allows a first and second admonition before rejection.

options.text: Let him keep dividing the church indefinitely.
options.note: The divisive man is self-condemned and must not be indulged forever.

quiz.q: What does Paul want those who have believed God to devote themselves to?

options.text: Good works, which are excellent and profitable for everyone.
options.note: Verse 8 urges believers to devote themselves to good deeds.

options.text: Endless debates about genealogies and the law.
options.note: Paul calls those controversies pointless and worthless, verse 9.

options.text: Earning their salvation through effort.
options.note: Good works flow from grace received, not to earn salvation.

options.text: Private religion with no visible fruit.
options.note: The fruit is public, profitable good works.

questions: Paul says gentleness toward everyone flows from remembering what we once were. How does recalling your own rescue change the way you treat difficult or hostile people?
Salvation here is entirely God's merciful work, not our righteous deeds. Where are you still tempted to base your standing before God on your own performance?
God poured out His Spirit on us abundantly. In what area of life do you most need to lean on the Spirit's renewing work right now?
Believers are to devote themselves to good works that are profitable to others. What concrete good work is God prompting you toward in your community this week?
Paul warns against pouring energy into pointless controversies and divisions. Is there a quarrel you need to step away from so you can invest in what actually builds up the church?

translationNotes.note: The washing of new birth translates the Greek for regeneration, as the BSB footnote notes; it pictures the Spirit's cleansing, life-giving renewal of the sinner.
This saying is trustworthy is one of the trustworthy sayings of the Pastoral Epistles, marking the preceding gospel summary as a settled, reliable confession.
